newsitem.title: FRANCE: France distributes iodine pills in N-plant area.
newsitem.headline: France distributes iodine pills in N-plant area.

text.p: France launched a doomsday health campaign on Monday by distributing iodine pills to people near a nuclear plant to help protect them from possible cancers in the event of radioactive leaks.

People in the southeastern towns of Saint-Maurice-L'Exil and Saint-Alban, close to a nuclear power station, were able to pick up iodine tablets from pharmacies, doctors' surgeries or town halls from Monday with a prescription sent to 2,500 homes.

Citizens are meant to keep the pills in a medicine cabinet and only take them if instructed by the local authorities after a nuclear leak. Hundreds of thousands of the tablets are already stocked in hospitals.

The campaign, the first of its type in France, would be gradually extended to 50,000 people living around the plant, run by state electricity utility EDF. Iodine aims to protect against thyroid cancers in the event of a nuclear leak.

By the end of 1996, everyone living within 10 km (six miles) of a nuclear plant in France is due to get the pills under a plan announced around the 10th anniversary of the Chernobyl disaster in April by Health Minister Herve Gaymard.
The pills are meant to saturate the thyroid with non-radioactive iodine and prevent the gland from absorbing any of the chemical in its radioactive form released by a nuclear accident.

"People have been trickling in steadily this morning," said Anne Roche at the Saint-Maurice-l'Exil town hall, where two students were distributing pills to locals in a room normally reserved for weddings.
Environmentalists have generally welcomed the iodine plan, but some say it is a gimmick to give French people a false sense of security about the potential dangers of nuclear energy.
The 1986 explosion at the Chernobyl plant, the world's worst nuclear accident, led to a rise in thyroid cancers near the plant in what is now Ukraine.
Lacking its own energy resources, France generates about 75 percent of its electricity from nuclear power, one of the highest rates in the world.

Opinion polls show atomic power is widely accepted in France, both for generating energy and in nuclear weapons. Domestic protests against French nuclear tests in the South Pacific a year ago were muted compared to those in many foreign nations.
